respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise depuis le grec (zoo82/1g), verification humaine requise

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo82/1g.xml (encodage Zoomathia, equipe/Mistral), lui-meme deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Le decoupage en 21 chapitres est une organisation thematique de la traductrice/du traducteur (Claude), calquee sur les divisions naturelles du texte source (reperes "livre.chapitre" d'Oppien, ex. 4.1, 5.1...), le fichier grec source ne comportant pas de decoupage en chapitres numerotes coherent. Les courtes notices factuelles repetees et intercalees dans le texte grec source (formule recurrente "le crocodile se trouve en...", sans lien avec le recit d'Eutecnius environnant) ont ete omises : elles semblent appartenir a une source de reference distincte melangee par erreur d'encodage au texte d'Eutecnius, et non a la paraphrase elle-meme.

div.head: Net-fishing: the sole, the dentex, and the tunny
div.p: The soles are drawn out, once caught, up onto the shore in their net.

For fish with fine bodies it is easy to pass clean through the net; but they are caught in another way. A kind of rage drives them, once they have fled, back toward the net, and they try to cut through it with their teeth; but it fastens itself upon them exactly, and does not let go as they are dragged. The dentex, on the other hand, swim in good order like men keeping the discipline of a watch, and do not approach a cast hook, but flee the moment they see it, until one of them, breaking rank, snatches the bait; then all at once take heart together, rejoicing with one another over the food, and hasten of their own accord to the catch.

Ocean gives birth to the tunny, and after their mating the spring leads them out into the rest of the sea. The most accomplished hunters of them are first the Iberians, and after them the Celts, who once dwelt in the land of Phocis (they live along the river Eridanus), and after these the Sicilians, whom the island of Trinacria nurtures beside the Tyrrhenian sea; and passing Sicily they range over every sea. The catching of them is the finest sport of all for fishermen: choosing a stretch of sea neither too narrow nor overhung with shadowy banks nor exposed to every wind, but well lit and having certain hollows, they station a skilled lookout upon some high headland; he surveys their number and reports the count, and at once the nets are stretched out on every side over the water like a city — the nets have gates, and guards of the gates, and very many chambers; and the men rush in as fast as they can, like ranks of soldiers, young and old and those in their prime, for as long as the net can hold them as they press forward, so that this is by far the most abundant of all forms of the hunt.

div.head: Love as bait for fish
div.p: Fish too desire mating without restraint, and this passion becomes their bait, whenever love, falling heavily upon them, destroys those it has seized. But if you should wish, O King, guiding with a calm sceptre, together with your son, all that lies beneath the sun, to grant a share of that same gentleness which is native to you to these writings as well, we for our part shall certainly offer our thank-offerings to the Muses, gladdening the lords of all things with their gifts.

"O Love, most cunning of the gods, sweetest to the eyes, yet sending unseen through them the passion into the soul, gentler than nothing, more violent even than fire itself — how you confound and trouble the reasoning mind, forcing it to suffer beyond measure, to shed frequent tears and groan under your goad, to grow pale and downcast, and by the hollowness of the eyes to proclaim the inward disturbance and sickness. Be gracious, though you feast on so many misfortunes of men, whom often, pressing hard upon them, you have compelled to die of necessity; whether we are to believe you the father of marriages and eldest of the gods, sprung forth before all the rest from Chaos itself, armed with that most excellent torch, or born of Aphrodite, so swift and winged — be mild and gracious to us; for who would willingly flee one so moderate? Who does not both love and shudder at the strength of him who has filled all things exactly with himself, who has, together with the gods, subdued mankind, and who, having well aimed his shaft even at the beasts, and having contended, since all that the air nurtures has bowed to his nod, extended his weapons even to the sea, and taught the fish that nothing is more powerful than love."

div.head: The parrot-wrasse and its constancy
div.p: This above all may be learned from the parrot-wrasse, who will not endure, even in the direst peril, to be parted from one another. If one of them takes the wound of the hook, at once another runs to the line, eager to bite it through and free the captive as quickly as possible — a thing which greatly vexes the fisherman. And if the weel-trap catches one of these fish, the captive contrives its own escape, watching carefully for the barbs of the cords, which fishermen are accustomed to weave at the entrances of the weels, curving inward, so that the fish once taken may not easily get out. For the wrasse sees these from within and fears them, as though they were guards keeping careful watch at the doors, and struggles to swim back out the way it came, putting forward its tail instead of its head, to spare its eyes. And the others, seeing it in this distress, now draw it out, seizing it by the mouth of its tail, now stretch out their own tails as guides, allowing it to bite and pass through together with them, and thus escape — closely imitating men hastening to reach a mountain peak in the night and the dark, who, clasping hands, pull and guide one another up. This love has furnished fishermen with a device against the wrasses; for four men, boarding a boat, share out the work in the following way.

div.head: Catching wrasses and mullets by decoy
div.p: Two keep steadily to the oars, while the third, having tied a female wrasse to a hook and fastened it to a line, and having put behind it a round and not very light piece of lead, tows it living through the sea, or rather makes a show of it as living, making it nod and bob by means of the lead — which the fishermen call the "dolphin" — which he sets into the mouth of the dead fish. Thereupon the wrasses, doing what is their nature, and pricked by love's darts, hasten from every side toward the female, following alongside the boat, however hard those appointed to row may pull. And the fourth man, holding a weel, when he judges that the moment for the catch has come, casts that round piece of lead into the weel with great force; and pressing down behind it and setting the weel upright, he shuts the female within; and the males, eager to reach their beloved, in their rivalry fill the trap, rushing in a body and forcing the entrance, like men contending for speed of foot and hastening toward the end of the racecourse, where the victor must reach the goal before the rest and bind on the longed-for crown of victory.

Some, putting a living female wrasse into a weel, catch a great many others besides, by fastening the weel to a rock inhabited by very many such fish. For, caught by the passion of love, they receive death in exchange for their fair desire — just as we know birds too are caught: those whose business is this kind of hunting prepare snares, and, placing within them a single bird well trained to deceive its own kind, and covering the place with bushes, draw in many more, luring them with the female's call.

In this same way fishermen also catch grey mullet, showing them a well-fed and sleek female, at the sight of whom the mullets, even if they should be drawn right out of the sea that nurtures them, as though ready to bear even the dry land for her sake, pay no heed to whatever devices the fishermen bring against them; one might say that they are like young men who, at the sight of a comely girl, are so smitten that, dazzled by the beauty of her eyes, at first they wish only to look upon it from afar, but then, little by little, as the flame of love grows within them, draw near and are unwilling to be parted, and no longer walk as they did before, but wherever the woman may lead. So too the mullets, blinded by their sickness, are enveloped when the fisherman lets down his casting-net.

div.head: The cuttlefish, and love's bait for other fish
div.p: For the cuttlefish, fishermen need neither weel nor seine-net; they use a plain and simple device: tying one cuttlefish to the waves by a thread, they let it down from the boat. The rest, seeing it carried along at random, leap upon it all together and wrap themselves exactly about it with their tentacles, like maidens who rejoice at the sight of a long-absent brother, or the one who begot them, returning safe, or like a woman newly tasted of marriage and passionately in love with her husband, who through the whole night winds her arms about him in an embrace; so too the cuttlefish, clinging to the one shown them, are unwilling to be parted, and are drawn up onto the boat. And if, when spring is bright, one should set upon the shore a weel shaded all about with leaves of the strawberry-tree or branches of tamarisk, or of some other plant that shows the season, it will gather the greatest swarm of cuttlefish, as though into some chamber suited to mating and repose, and so will draw up the trap full.

The wretched blackbird, too, received the flame of love for the thrushes. For sickness compels it to be jealous and to wear itself out keeping watch over many, since it will not settle down with one alone. Hence it must forever attend upon a great many ravines; and the thrushes dare not so much as look out from them, just as the women of the women's quarters, whom no one has ever yet seen come forth, are still, as it were, blushing at the thought of living with men; and so the thrushes cannot be seen, whom the blackbird compels to remain within — for he is forever roaming about them all, for the sake of keeping exact watch over his beloveds, and wishes to see nothing else, mastered by jealousy more than by hunger, unless night, appearing, should grant him a little time for food and a little rest, lulling to sleep his ill-starred anxiety. And if the thrushes are about to lay their eggs, who would not pity the blackbird, seeing him hurrying to look upon them all, prevailing by his labours on their behalf over each one and troubled at heart, like the mother of an only daughter watching her child suffer the unaccustomed pangs of labour — for then the mother too is pierced with pains no less than she who is in labour, and, unable even to bear the sight of the girl for fear, roams about the chamber praying, groaning, and as it were beside herself, until some cry announces to her from within that the birth-pangs are loosed.

They say the sons of the Assyrians, who dwell beyond the Tigris, and the Bactrian people (who are the best of all at archery), are driven mad in just this way over their women: for each of them has many wives, and at night the wives come in turn to their husbands; and the men are so overcome by jealousy that they even choose to make war upon those who have wronged them; for nothing is more painful than jealousy, nor is there any greater occasion for calamity, nor does any other madness so compel men to lamenting and raving, even to the point of death. This too has furnished fishermen with their bait against the blackbird: watching the blackbird doing his own work about the dwellings of the thrushes, they fasten a living shrimp to a hook, and, putting on it a not very light piece of lead, let down the hook above it. The blackbird, thinking that the shrimp is scheming against his marriage (for the fisherman often stirs the bait against the rock), rushes at it with great force, as though about to tear it apart at once with his beak, but in his passion, hastening toward destruction, knows nothing of it. For once he has taken in the hook, when the fisherman, raising the line, is satisfied that it is firmly fixed in him, he is drawn up with great speed; and then one might imagine the fisherman, laughing, saying some such thing as this: "It is high time, you wretch, that you had looked to guarding your household before now; high time you revelled in your many marriages, staying at home to tend your swarm of females; but you shall prove a very fine bridegroom with us too, once you have made acquaintance with the flame." These things he will say in jest to one who perceives nothing of it. And it is then easy to catch the thrushes; for, abandoning the rocks, they wander about freely, unguarded.

div.head: The octopus and the olive branch; the sargue and the goat
div.p: Not only in these ways does love make sport of the fish, forcing them to rage after one another, but it also destroys them by casting into them strange desires for other things. Desire for the olive tree draws the octopus even out of the sea. It is a wonderful thing to see, its branches loved as truly as one's own children; for whenever some place by the sea nurtures an olive tree, the octopus perceives it, catching the scent as dogs do, which the perception through their nostrils leads, guiding their masters, to the tracks and lairs of wild beasts; and running out of the sea, the octopus, though a fish, creeps with delight even upon the land, and, first flinging itself upon the root, imitates a young man who, when his nurse appears after a long absence, throws his arms about her, now rolling in her lap, now clasping her neck. Thence, running up onto the branches (its tentacles, taking hold of the olive, easily draw it up to the height), it goes about each branch as though to kiss it, and one might liken it to a man who, after a long journey abroad, embraces his agemates as they stand around him in a circle; and just as we see the ivy, poured about the branches of the fir from the root to the summit, running upward, so too the octopus, sated with its beloved, hastens back again to the sea. And the craftsmen of this hunt, having learned this passion, have contrived from it a bait: binding olive branches together, and placing a piece of lead between them so that they may not easily be carried off elsewhere by the waves, and hanging them from the boat, they draw up the octopuses by means of them; for as soon as they appear, the octopuses rush upon the leaves and are unwilling to be parted, even when they are being drawn up into the fishermen's hands.

This same love, joining together things separated by nature, forces the sargue-fish to rage after goats, and sends lovers out of the sea toward the flocks, to whom the hills are a beloved dwelling-place. For whenever, as the season grows warm under the sun's ray, the herdsmen who love the sargues drive their goats down to the shore to wash them, the sargues hear the bleating and, seized by its foul reek, no longer delay, sluggish though they are, but gathering quickly, hasten toward their beloveds, following alongside the boat, fawning upon them and licking at them, they leap for joy, and astonish the shepherds who first behold it; for the kids do not look with more pleasure upon their mothers returning from pasture. And when the shepherds lead their flocks back from the sea to the folds, the sargues make a calamity of the parting and follow along the shore as far as they can. And who would not laugh to see a fish following out of love? Or who would not think he beheld a mother or a wife, parting from her son or her husband with the greatest weeping, imploring that he return as quickly as possible, reckoning the length of the sea and of the time, gazing fixedly out at the deep, unwilling to go back into the house? One might even say that the sargues weep, being parted from the goats. This has taught fishermen to master with ease these hapless fish, which dwell by twin rocks, kept apart by a narrow channel through which the sun makes the height of water warm; for these fish delight exceedingly in the rays of the sun.

div.head: Catching the sargue by a goat-disguise; the sargues' own jealousy
div.p: The craftsman of this device, taking possession of one of the rocks, brings to the fish as a bait the likeness of a goat, their beloved: putting on a goat's hide and showing horns raised up from his head, and mixing in barley-meal blended with goat's fat and flesh, so that, their sight and their perception together being deceived, they are persuaded that their beloved is present on every side — and so he persuades the whole gathered company to hasten toward what they suppose it to be. And putting a piece of this flesh on the hook, he draws up, with all his strength and speed, whichever sargue is caught, hoping to catch as many as possible, if by deceiving them one at a time he can each time keep it hidden from the rest, but otherwise, if he should be found out, to labour in vain; for if they perceive the deception, they would not come near even if the actual goats stood by, and would abandon their familiar rock.

The sargues are jealous of one another too, and the males fight over the females; and the one who prevails in the fight lives with them at his pleasure, for he drives off the vanquished and shuts the females up among the rocks beneath the sea. Fishermen, having learned this by experience, fence a weel about on every side exactly with branches of myrtle or bay, hiding the trap entirely. The sargue, thinking he sees a rock and not a weel, puts into it those many females he has carried off as plunder, and the weel is at once filled as the fish are driven in; and he who put them in, having kept off the vanquished, follows last and is caught after his victory. So it is the custom among shepherds, whenever they lead the flock back from pasture to the fold, to look about to see whether all their charges are safe, and to be the last to enter the steading. Such are the pranks that love plays upon the fish.

div.head: Fish that follow shipwrecks; catching the coryphaena
div.p: To the coryphaena the remains of shipwrecked men are a welcome food; and they run eagerly toward ships which the storm of the sea has broken apart, and busy themselves about the scattered planks, and are easily caught close by them, if someone should come upon them and fish there. But may the god of the sea keep from sailors the danger, and may the ships be carried safely through the waves and bring home their cargoes. There is also another way of catching the coryphaena, and this device has been discovered against them: binding together bundles of reeds, they let them go upon the waves, having put a stone among the reeds; and the coryphaena run up to the fronds of the reeds and rub their backs against them, and so are caught by hooks, vying with one another and hastening toward the bait, just like dogs, whom one may see gaping toward whatever food is given, leaping forward eagerly ahead of one another, fixing their eyes on the hand of the giver and showing their rivalry with their teeth. It is then great toil for the fishermen to draw up as quickly as possible those they catch, for the fish do not come to the bait in order, but are caught with great eagerness. And the pilot-fish suffer the same fate as the coryphaena, being lovers of shade just as they are.

div.head: The eel, and the shoal of anchovies
div.p: The eels are nurtured by harbours, and the following game has been devised against them by the young: they let down into the water a long sheep's gut, like a fishing-line; then they watch to see if some eel, running up, bites the gut, and immediately blowing into it, they swell it up, and stretch the fish's mouth with their breath, so that it cannot spit out the gut, and so draw up their catch, just as men drawing wine with a reed by breath from the largest jars.

As for the anchovy, which is ever accompanied by fear and flight, one could not catch it alone; for very many of them, flowing together into a single mass, hold fast to one another exactly, intertwined, so that not even a boat can sail through them, but is checked as though by a rock, nor can they be parted from one another even by oars striking them, nor could anyone ever part them even with an axe; for whoever strikes into them, cutting some through the head and others through the tail, and dividing others through the middle, in no way breaks up their mass by this. One might gather them up in one's hands as though they were sand all mixed together, and, casting a seine-net about them, take one's fill of the catch, filling both the boat and the shore, heaping up mounds of fish — just as farmers gather wheat onto the threshing-floor, when, having cut the grain now ripe, they toss it to the wind with winnowing-fans, showing the threshing-floor white, just as the sea is seen made white by the anchovy.

div.head: The bonito: their spawning-ground and their hunt in the Bosporus
div.p: Let us speak also of the bonito, both of their spawning and of the region that receives it: it is the Euxine Sea, where the Maeotic Lake flows in, nurturing very many reeds, beside which the tunnies, having spawned, devour their own young. But those of the eggs that escape become the bonito, which, leaving their father's sea, hasten to the Thracian strait, as the deepest of all waters in the open sea, and one whose bottom is never in the least disturbed by the winds, and which has the most abundant mud and grass, sufficient for the food of the very young fish. There the bonito, plunging in, escape the chill of the sea, which often robs them even of their sight. But when spring comes on, they mingle with one another, and return to their father's sea, if they can escape the dreadful hunt of the Thracians, whose manner is as follows: the fishermen pour a small piece of lead into the end of a thick stick a cubit long, and, fixing close-set barbs into it, hang it from a very long and strong cord able to bear the weight. Thus, putting out into the deepest part of the sea toward the Bosporus, they let down the stick, which, driven by its own weight, plunges to the bottom; and it falls into the very swarm of the bonito, which lies exactly in the mud, and pierces very many of them with its barbs, and so they are drawn up — a terrible and pitiable sight among fish, even for one who is not without pity; for one is struck on the head, another wounded in the flank, another pierced through the tail, another run through the belly, another bears the point through its back, and another has its side torn open — the fearsome image of a battle and of wounds, such as those bring home who, after wars, gather the dead and carry the remains to the pyre with lamentation; yet this hunt too delights the fishermen.

Others catch the bonito with nets, in the following manner: these fish above all dread disturbances in the dark, and if someone at night should stir some commotion in the water, they go down into the depths to hide themselves. So these men, enclosing a bay with nets, make a great noise, at one time rowing with a great shout, at another striking the water with their oars and disturbing the bonito, and so compel them to make for the net, as though it were some safe place, sufficient for their escape from the tumult; and thus through folly they are caught while trying to avoid the noise. Then one might marvel at the speed and eagerness of the fishermen together, as they haul in the ropes and the nets together with the fish. For the bonito, terrified at the sight of the ropes, lie heaped together upon one another, unless some ill fortune should thwart the fishermen by having one leap up and show the way out through the net; for if one should escape, the rest will certainly follow. Something similar has been contrived by men whose business is this hunt, against deer too (and this is as timid a creature as any): they surround with ropes a place thick with plants, all round in a circle, and hang feathers from them, so that they are stirred by the wind, and the sight easily frightens the deer, and so they are caught with ease.

div.head: Frightening the sargues and the meagre; disguise-hunting
div.p: Fishermen also catch the sargues by frightening them, even without showing any bait, and the meagre in the same way. For the sargues, if they take fright upon reaching the bottom, pack themselves exactly together, lying on their sides, and raise the spines upon their backs, so that no one may easily lay a hand on them — just as farmers are accustomed to do, fencing their threshing-floors about with stakes so as to keep off thieves from their harvest. But those who are accustomed to venture most boldly to the bottom and swim beneath the waves, diving down into the deep, and, seeing the sargues packed together, look carefully about their heads and tails; then, laying their hands upon the heads and pressing down upon them thus while they lie still, they catch them, the fish trusting in vain in the sharpness of their spines; for carrying one sargue in each hand, they rise to the surface, while the rest lie as they were gathered. The meagre, when fear falls upon it, flees to some rock, or a bed of some hollow, or a gully, or else hides its head beneath some plant, forgetful, as it were, of the rest of its body — just as the hartebeest is accustomed to do when fleeing the lion, thrusting its head into a thicket, as though, not seeing the lion itself, it were certainly unseen; so too, even when caught and torn, it persists in clinging to its own device. There is also a creature nurtured by Libya, the largest of birds, putting forth a long neck, using its feathers not so much for flying as for a similar device in dangers to that of the hartebeest; for it thinks that if it hides its head it escapes the notice of hunters. The fisherman, laughing at the meagre for thinking the same, will draw it out of its lair. Such are the devices fishermen contrive against these fish; but the hunt of all the rest

is pursued in common, by nets, weels, hooks, or even tridents, throughout the whole day and on into the evening; for about the first hours of the night the hunters kindle a fire and go out upon the sea, and easily spear with their tridents those fish which, delighting in the flame, rush upon the boat.

div.head: Poisoning fish out of their lairs
div.p: But some destroy the fish with a drug and so catch them, first driving them together and gathering them into certain hollows with a great many casts of lead weights, or with poles, or with oars; and having thus taken refuge in a single place, they surround them with nets, just as men besieging a city surround it with a ring of wall. Then, when this seems to them well done, someone, taking the most oily plant, which they call "clay-plant," and another root, which physicians call cyclamen, and making cakes from both, leaps down close to the place that holds the fish, before the nets are drawn, and smears the lairs and the dens with the drug, and, having filled the very sea with its foul smell, hastens back again to the boat. Thereupon one may see the wretched fish overcome by the smell, so that they cannot even remain in the dens where they were hiding, but rush out, their heads heavy and their sight dimmed; then, finding the sea itself much worse because of the drug, they wheel about, like men overcome by drunkenness, for whom, as they are carried round in a circle, there is no firm footing; and so, overcome by the evil, the fish fall into the nets, nothing availing for their safety, even though they leap up again and again in their rush, and stir up the whole sea, disturbing the water with their last gasps, by which they show their agony. The fishermen, meanwhile, delighting in this, keep still, until the fish, being destroyed and no longer troubling the water by their continual thrashing, the sea grows calm; for then they draw them out, dead by this common manner of death. Those besieging a city are accustomed to poison the springs for just such a purpose, in order to crush those within by hunger and hardship and the foulness of the water, since, when the dead are being destroyed in various ways, the whole city must of necessity be filled with them. Thus, by means of drugs, hunters bring a bitter death upon the fish.

div.head: On human mastery over animals
div.p: From all this, then, mightiest King, you must reckon that nothing is beyond the reach of men's daring, whether they must labour upon the land or upon the sea; but we are a race set somewhat below the gods in power — whether it was Prometheus, whom they say to be the son of Iapetus, who, mixing water with earth and anointing our hearts with some divine unguent, made mankind a creature equal to the gods, or whether we are sprung from the gore of the Titans, inferior to the gods alone. For men master even the beasts that are strong in the mountains, and, walking on foot, catch birds that are close upon the very clouds; and neither its boldness saves the lion, nor its flight rescue the eagle; and the greatest of all creatures upon the earth, the elephant, mightiest in the strength of its black trunk, they force to go beneath the yoke and do the work of mules; and they destroy even the monsters of the sea, in no way weaker than the flesh-devouring beasts of the land, but surpassing them, whether one examines their size, or their boldness, or their strength — as must now be considered.

div.head: The great sea-monster: seals and their fear of it
div.p: We know that the seals themselves, even on land, fear such creatures, and, closing with them, are everywhere overcome, the beasts of the sea being stronger. Yet neither their monstrous nature nor their strength suffices against the schemes of men, but they are destroyed by fishermen, as I shall tell; listen graciously to what follows.

The greatest of the sea-monsters feed in the midst of the open sea and for the most part do not come up to the surface, but keep close to the very bottom of the sea, and desire food without restraint (for what could ever be sufficient, or whence?), knowing no satiety, yet suffering from hunger; and they must make war upon one another, and the vanquished becomes food for the victor. The sight of a ship, too, frightens them, especially in the Iberian sea, where they leave the neighbouring Ocean, in which some are equal in size even to ships of twenty oars. And often, straying onto shoals near the shore, they are carried ashore, and it is then above all that they may be overcome; for all the great ones, except the dog-fish kind, are sluggish, and, because of their bulk, ill-suited to flight; for they neither see far off, nor go readily out into the open sea, being weighed down by their own size, and press through the water only with difficulty and little by little. For this reason a small fish serves as a guide to them all — one with a long body and a slender tail. It is called the "leader," and is beloved by the sea-monsters, keeping company with them and standing guard, being the only creature they trust, leading them wherever it wishes, and for the sake of guiding them turning its tail before the monsters' very eyes,

and thus steers the sea-monster, either sharing the same origin of birth with it, or joined to it by understanding alone. So it is that neither beauty nor strength is of any use unless understanding attend it, but strength without sense destroys its possessor as something vain and useless, while good counsel saves even the very smallest — for which reason the great sea-monster makes even this small fish its own guardian.

div.head: How fishermen hunt the great sea-monster
div.p: First, then, one must deceive and catch the fish by putting food around a hook; for in no other way could one overcome the sea-monster, but once caught it will easily be taken, since it knows neither how to run back to its lair, nor to avoid the harm now close upon it, but is carried along without purpose, like a ship that has lost its helmsman, so that it is often driven onto a rock or the shore, a great mist being spread over its eyes. Having then made their prayer, the hunters set about the catch just as men who fall upon their enemies by night, and, if they should overcome the guards, go boldly against the citadel itself, eager to set fire to the houses. As for its size and weight, they judge in the following way: if it barely shows above the sea, revealing its ridge or its hump, the beast is of monstrous size and is scarcely borne up by the sea; but if even its back should be seen, they say it swims but a little above the surface because of its lightness.

The fishing-line they use is of the closest-woven cords, and its length is like the forestays of ships, being neither altogether small nor overly great; a strong hook is fastened to the line, having close-set barbs on every side, such as could take firm hold even of a rock, curved in such a way as to be swallowed when the sea-monster gapes; and a heavy bronze chain is joined to it, so that it may be able to bear the edge of the monster's teeth, and wheels divide the chain in a circle, so that it may neither twist upon itself nor be broken clean through by the monster straining under the pain, but rather, as the creature wanders in a circle, be drawn round more easily. Then they set upon the hook a liver or shoulder of a bull, of a size fitting so great a gape, and, boarding many small boats, and arming themselves with darts and tridents, and carrying with them ox-goads and sickles and very many other things forged for this purpose, they signal to one another in silence what must be done, not even striking too loudly with their oars; for if the sea-monster should perceive them, by diving down it will make their toil in vain. Drawing near, they let down the chain together with the food, and the sea-monster, rushing upon it, seizes and is caught,
and, in its pain, pulls back against it, and, unable to break it, dives toward the bottom, the fishermen giving way.

div.head: The battle with the sea-monster: skin-floats, and the killing
div.p: For they would sooner be dragged down themselves, boats and all, than haul up the sea-monster against its will; so they contrive some such device as this: filling very broad skins with air and fastening them to the line, they let them down, and the monster drags them along by force until it reaches the very bottom; then there, like horses which, breathing hot, spit forth foam and blood through their bit, it spends its time in pain; and it is drawn up again by the skins to the surface of the sea, the air pushing them.

Then the men are eager to seize it too, but in vain; for, trying to bite it, they escape it, as though alive, swerving aside; then, in pain, it dives down again, and does this many times, pulling and being pulled back in turn, just as men who have taken up the common labour of sawing wood, in order to prepare the keel of a ship or something else; for they take hold of the rough saw as it is set upon the wood and passes through it with a grinding sound, and the completed stroke is drawn back again in the opposite direction. Such is the contest, as it were, between the skins and the sea-monster, and it, in its pain, sends blood into the sea, and breathes heavily, and churns the water with its blowing, as though a great quantity of breath lay hidden beneath the sea, and, breathing, produces certain whirlings and swellings of the water, such as one may see about Charybdis, whenever the wind troubles the strait formed by the parting of the mountains, upon which, when the winds drive them, the Ionian and the Tyrrhenian seas are borne.

Then it is also a good moment for the fishermen to run to the shore and fasten the boat to some rock, until the beast, exhausted by its own rushings and counter-pullings, yields, taking some notion of its end; for then one of the skins rises up, a clear proof of the beast's defeat. And the fishermen look upon it with pleasure, as men beholding, after a war, a herald clad in white and gaping eagerly for the good news he brings; then at once they see the other skins too, dragging some great creature, overcome by pain and toil, and they drive their boats onward, raising a great shout and clamour, calling to one another as though in war; for such is the eagerness that possesses them then, that if some goatherd, or hunter, or woodcutter should hear them from afar, he would certainly, in his astonishment, run down to the shore and watch what was happening. One strikes it with a trident, another with a dart; another wields a sickle, another kills it with an ox-goad, and all, like armed soldiers, hurl and strike the beast at close range. And it, forgetting its measureless strength, can no longer hold back the ships with its jaws, but, driving the water with the thrust of its fins, pushes back the boats as though some contrary wind were blowing, and is overcome amid a very great shout, and dyes the sea with gore, as when a torrent, rushing down from some red hills, colours red the whole bay over which it runs.

And they pour vinegary wine upon its wounds, so that, burning, the beast is destroyed the sooner; one might say a ship had been struck by a thunderbolt and set ablaze, and that the fire, coming near the water, blazed up all the more.

div.head: The death of the sea-monster and its aftermath
div.p: As it is about to breathe its last, overcome by its wounds, they bind it and drag it toward the land, pierced through with many barbs, and row rejoicing greatly and singing right nobly, like men who have been victorious in a sea-battle and have bound the enemy's ships and, shouting loudly over their victory and singing paeans, drag along the vanquished, unwilling and disheartened.

As it draws near the shore, it convulses in its last throes and lashes the sea and turns about, like birds slaughtered upon altars that wish, in their last movements, to fly up again toward the sky but have no strength for it. It is then drawn onto the land like some enormous ship, which sailors, so that it may not labour when a storm comes on, drag with great toil, so that it may not be worn by the winter; so too the greatest of sea-monsters, once laid upon the land, fills the shore, and after its death is a most dreadful sight to behold.

One might be afraid even of it dead, and be thrown into confusion at the unlovely sight of the sea-monster, looking especially at its dreadful teeth; but at last, taking courage, men gather together and look closely at the remains of the beast, some astonished at the ranks of teeth set in its jaws, beholding the tusks, like javelins, growing in triple rows; others gazing at the wounds and the size of the injuries, another at the sharp spine and the barbs standing up from it, another at the tail and its capacity,

others at the belly, and not a few at the enormous head, so that someone unaccustomed to sailing, but living upon the land, struck with terror at the sight of the beast, might say some such thing as this to those nearby: "May it be granted to me, born and raised upon the land, to fulfil my last day upon it, kept apart from the labours of the sea, honouring from the land the might of the sea-god, and may I never, trusting a little plank, sail, nor look about at the winds and the clouds in this way; for I have no desire for seafaring, nor for the hardships which sailors endure amid the ill-sounding storms;

nor is it enough to meet such an end, but one must also be devoured, and fill, instead of a tomb, the belly of some such beast; so that fear of the thing possesses me, and I wish, from the land, to address the sea, that it may be gracious to me from afar." So the greatest of the sea-monsters are hunted in this manner; but the toil against the lesser ones is less, and the gear suited to the hunt is proportioned to it: shorter lines and hooks, and not much bait, and, instead of goatskins, the hollow shells of a dry gourd, by means of which, as has been said, the beast will be drawn up.

div.head: The young shark, and the seal
div.p: If ever the cub of a shark should be seen, the fishermen, having shown it the oar-thong repeatedly beforehand (for so they call the bindings of the oars), catch the cub as it rushes upon it; for once it has bitten, its teeth, being curved, must of necessity be caught fast in it, so that it is most easily killed with a trident.

Among all the most hostile of the sea-monsters are the dog-fish, of which we have said there are several kinds; they are fierce, bold, reckless, fearless, and rabid, so that they often even damage the nets and the weels, if they should come near them, and spoil the catch itself; for they devour the fish, so that they too are sometimes caught by fishermen out of love of food, and by the hook.

As for the seals, it is not easy to catch them even with a hook, nor to kill them readily with a trident; for their hides are exceedingly strong and would not easily be torn through; but if, against their will, together with the other fish, they should be enclosed with a net, the fishermen haul them with all speed toward the shore altogether; for the seal, straining eagerly, tears the nets with the sharp edges of its claws, so that it is no small grief to the fishermen when it escapes, just as the rest of the fish that have been caught also escape. Drawn out and brought near to land, they destroy it with clubs and other pieces of wood, and with the trident besides; and it will die most quickly if struck about the temples and the head.

div.head: The turtle, and the golden rule of the sea
div.p: And the turtles too, which damage the catch and harm the fishermen themselves, are easy to take, if only one is bold and unafraid; for one must go under it and turn it over, and turn the shell that had covered it round toward the sea; and then it is no longer easy for it, however much it might wish, to right itself again, but it will labour, thrashing and moving its feet to no purpose, and be laughed at, so that the fishermen are able to drag it off tied with a noose, and to kill it with iron. For it is no different from the land tortoises, which children in the mountains often overturn, laughing at their legs as they wave about, when the creature is helpless to right itself and, wishing to turn onto its belly, has not the strength. And this too must be known about the sea-turtles: that when they come out onto the land they are often scorched by the sun, so that, returning again to the sea, they cannot even dive down, because of the dryness of their shells, and are thus most easily caught by the fishermen.

div.head: On not killing dolphins: Arion and the boy of Poroselene
div.p: To catch dolphins must be reckoned an impious thing, and no one, daring this, could sacrifice in holiness, or stand at an altar; but he who does this is accursed, and a pollution to those who share his roof, and would seem no different from a murderer, whoever should knowingly destroy a dolphin. So greatly do they enjoy the favour of the god of the sea, and they are friends to one another, and often are helpers to men in the hunting of fish. In the island of Euboea, for instance, in the Aegean sea, when fishermen are busy with the evening catch and make use of fire,

shutting it up in some hollow bronze vessel, dolphins too are present together with the fish, not allowing them to dive to the bottom, but driving them onto the land, like hunting dogs pursuing with their baying the beasts that appear, so that the fishermen are able to spear with the trident the fish that have turned toward the shore in fear; for the fish cannot fight both the fire and the dolphins at once. And the dolphins, when the hunt is finished, ask a fee, drawing near the boats, and receive a certain share, since, if they did not receive it, they would no longer help the men in the hunt at all.

And indeed the ancient tale would have it that Arion of Lesbos too escaped death, which certain pirates were bringing upon him, and, singing, came to Taenarum in Laconia, borne upon the back of a dolphin. They say, too, that a dolphin fell in love with a Libyan boy, and, delighting to come to the shore where he tended his flock, was so wildly eager to hear his pipe that it was ready even to leave the sea and mingle with the sheep. And of another youth's love, no ancient tale but a recent one,

the dolphin, coming often to the harbour of the island, welcomed his company as that of a companion; and being still a cub when it first came to love the boy, still a small child, it grew up together with him as he came of age, and was itself already full-grown while the youth was still young. This strange thing, beyond all telling and beyond all hope, held both strangers and citizens in wonder, and many flocked together from many places out of desire to see it, and a crowd of onlookers always stood upon the shore. For the boy, boarding a little boat and coming near the harbour, would call the dolphin by a certain name; and it, recognizing the name given to it from the first and the boy's voice,

would come most swiftly near the boat, fawning with its tail and raising its head and exulting, eager to touch the boy; and he, as though he were some beloved friend, would stroke the dolphin with his hands as it strove even to climb onto the boat. Then, when the boy dived in, they swam together, fitting head to head and side to side; and one might say the dolphin wished to kiss and embrace the youth, and for that reason chose to swim at an equal pace with him. Often, too, the boy, taking hold of the dolphin's dorsal fin, would leap upon its wet back,

and it, receiving this service with the greatest delight, welcomed it, going wherever the youth wished, whether toward the open sea, or toward the land or the harbour. What colt would ever be so obedient to the bridle, what dog so well trained would obey a huntsman leading it, or what soldier obey a general's command so readily as the dolphin obeyed the youth, carrying, apart from yoke or rein, not only him but also whomever else he bade it carry? So it loved the youth while he lived; but when he died, it came to the shore as though in mourning, seeking him, and, not finding its friend,
grieving greatly, no longer came at the islanders' call, nor would it accept food, and very quickly wasted away, and was no more seen about that place, having died of longing for the youth.

But even though the dolphins are so gentle, and know how to think as men do, the insolent Thracians hunt them, and so do the Byzantines, and one could not say that men so ruthless would spare children, or fathers, or brothers. For two cubs, born together, follow their mother, and neither flee an approaching boat nor suspect any trick, but, delighting in men, draw near them as companions; and the fishermen, with a trident (which they call the "barb," a light javelin), strike one of the two cubs as it draws near, and it, driven by pain

and suffering greatly, dives to the bottom, the sailors giving line, and, having fastened a very long cord to the trident (for otherwise they could not master the catch), row the boat with all speed, following wherever, in its pain, the creature makes for. And it, overcome by the wasting sickness and the pains, thrashing upon the barbs of the iron, is raised up, lifted by the waves, breathing its last;

but its mother does not abandon it, but follows, grieving greatly, and a mother whose sons are being dragged off after the capture of her city could not grieve more than she, suffering as though she herself

had been wounded; she drives off her other young and, rushing at it, pursues it away; and one might say she speaks to it thus: "Do you see, my child, how we are betrayed and warred upon, and that it is better to flee these impious men, since men are no longer friends to us either?" So, having driven off her other cub, she does not abandon the wounded one, not even if someone should wish to frighten or strike at her, until she draws near the hands of those hauling it in; and they, without pity, feel no compassion for her despairing grief, but, piercing her too with their sharp bronze barbs, kill her together with her young, though she was fully willing to be killed for its sake;

div.head: Two more images of grief; the divers who gather sponges
div.p: if a serpent, coming forth from beneath the eaves, should draw near the nestlings of a swallow, it devours them without pity, and the mother flies about at first as though in lament, but no longer wishes to flee once her young are lost, but, coming right to the jaws of the serpent, is herself devoured; so too, wishing to die over her dolphin-child, the mother is killed by the fishermen.

All shell-fish grow fat as the moon waxes, and, as it wanes again, grow weak and thin. Some are caught right from the sea-bottom, others clinging fast to the rocks; others the wave casts up onto the shore, and the hollowed sand covers them in certain pits. The greediest of shellfish are the purple-fish, and the manner of hunting them is as follows: weaving little creels, like baskets, out of close-set cords, and putting whelks inside them, they cast them down into the sea; and the purple-fish, drawing near, wishing to devour the whelks, stretch out their tongues (which are thin and sharp) through the cords to reach the food, and so, caught fast, are taken; for their tongues, swelling, can no longer come back out through the meshes, and pain now swells them further, until, the creel being drawn up, they are all caught, bound fast by their tongues — a fair and lovely flower for purple weavings.

Of the sponge-cutters, none could say that any other man labours more or runs greater danger. These men, when first setting out upon their contest, are content with little drink and a little food, and take not the sleep that is fitting for fishermen, but train themselves, as heralds who are about to compete are wont to do, oiling their voices, so that their breath may hold out for them at the bottom, and that they may bear without harm the toil that lies before them. As the contest draws near, having come to the middle of the sea and having prayed at great length that they may not encounter a sea-monster, or suffer some other harm, and if they see the "fair-fish" (for by that name they call it), taking the greatest courage, as though no sea-monster would harm them near this fish, which they therefore call sacred, believing that it feeds in common with them, they do the following: girding himself above the loins with a very long cord, one of them carries a piece of lead in his left hand, and holds out a sickle in his right, and, taking oil in his mouth, stands thus on the prow and looks out to sea, surveying the task and the depth of the water; and those standing by encourage him, as we are accustomed to urge on those about to contend in a foot-race.

And he, if he has taken courage, dives in headfirst and is drawn down by the lead to the bottom, and, having descended and spat out the oil, sees, by so much light as a fire would make at night, the sponges upon the rocks (which grow in the deepest places of the sea and, being alive, cling fast to the rocks like very many other things); and he holds out the sickle, and, like a reaper, cuts away the sponges, and at once hastens to signal to his companions, by the cord, that they must haul him up. They, without delay, all pull upon the cord, lest the discharge of the sponges reach the diver first, a thing so foul-smelling that it could even choke him; so that, drawn up, one might behold him with both pleasure and pity, worn out by fear and toil. Often, too, one of them, leaping into the sea, does not come up again, having fallen in with a sea-monster, but signals to his companions to haul up, and is already being devoured, and, hastening toward his companions and the ship, is torn apart by the sea-monster. And the others put in to land, bitterly grieving and lamenting the loss of their companion.

So much, most god-beloved King, do I know, having learned it, concerning the creatures of the sea; and may the sea remain ever abundant in fish for you, and may you rule over the land, its foundations rooted unshaken.
